2. What is this, in plain words

A cache is a notebook where a program writes down an answer so it does not have to work it out again. The risk is the notebook: it can fill up without end, it can be shared by the wrong people, or it can say something that is no longer true. Think of a hotel front desk that keeps a sticky note of every guest's room. If notes from hotel A are handed to a guest of hotel B, that is a data leak. If the notes are never thrown away, the desk disappears under paper. If the note still says "guest allowed in" an hour after the guest was removed, that is a security hole.

Glossary. Cache: a remembered answer. Redis: the shared fast memory server. TTL: time to live, how long a note lives. Tenant / workspace: one customer company. Org id: the number that names it. Bounded: has a size limit. Stale window: how long a changed fact can stay hidden. Stampede: many requests all recomputing the same missing answer at once. Fail closed / open: refuse, or carry on, when the store is down. Ratchet: a test that only lets things get better. P0: decides access, permissions, session, plan, money or holds credentials. P1: everything else.

3. How we tested

  1. Found every cache by searching for Redis writes (syntax tree), mutable Map/Set fields, Cache-Control headers, Next.js cache options and TanStack Query settings, then read each one.
  2. Wrote register.json: key, tenant, TTL, bound, invalidation, stampede, store failure, stale window, priority for every cache.
  3. Wrote ratchets that read the code and the register. Each was run on a bad example and failed (section 5).
  4. Wrote behaviour tests: workspace A then B with the same ids; a moving clock to measure stale seconds; Redis down, slow and losing one command; 50 parallel misses.
  5. For each defect: failing test first, then the smallest shared fix.
  6. Merged the latest main (including the Redis command timeout from #663), re-ran everything, and refreshed the register: the ratchets themselves caught two changes (knowledge-base cache, a new time-zone Map).

5. Findings

D-64-01 MEDIUM FIXED A counter could be created and never expire

What went wrong. Fifteen places counted with INCR and then, in a second command, set the expiry. If the second command was lost (dropped connection, crash, timeout) the counter lived for ever. For the failed-API-key counter, whose name has no time bucket, that locks the address out of the API permanently.

Why it matters. Anyone behind a shared address (an office, a mobile carrier) after a Redis blip.

How we fixed it. New helper incrWithTtl() sends INCR and EXPIRE NX in one transaction; all 15 call sites use it; a ratchet bans the old pattern.

Test that proves it. counter-ttl.spec.ts, ratchet.spec.ts

D-64-02 LOW FIXED In-process caches that only ever grew

What went wrong. About twenty caches keyed by workspace, target or time-zone name were checked for expiry on read but never trimmed. One (calendar feed zone names) is keyed by text a feed sender controls; one (message-feed time zone) was found by the ratchet after the merge with main.

Why it matters. Server memory over weeks; a hostile calendar feed could add entries at will.

How we fixed it. setCapped() and CappedMap evict the oldest entry at a cap (500 to 10 000, set per cache). A ratchet fails any new unbounded Map or Set.

Test that proves it. bounded-caches.spec.ts, ratchet.spec.ts

D-64-05 MEDIUM FIXED Signing out kept the browser cache of the old person

What went wrong. Five sign-out buttons used router.replace, which keeps the page running. The query cache (fresh 30 s, kept 5 min, keys without workspace or user) therefore survived, and the next person to sign in on the same tab saw the previous person's lists first. A helper that does a full navigation already existed but only three screens used it.

Why it matters. A second user on a shared computer; an operator signing in as another operator.

How we fixed it. All sign-outs (staff menu, operator shell, admin console, IP-blocked screen, password reset) go through signOut(), which navigates the whole page. A web ratchet fails any new fetch of a logout route that does not.

Test that proves it. user-menu.logout-cache.render.test.tsx, cache-audit.test.ts

R-64-01 LOW OPEN No single-flight on the P0 caches

50 parallel misses cause 50 recomputations for the account gate, workspace suspension, notification prefs and RBAC (measured). Each is one small query per concurrent request on expiry. Recommendation: share one in-flight promise per key, as analytics already does.

R-64-02 LOW OPEN Partner agent invalidate() has no caller

Nothing in the API changes a partner agent's status today, so the 30 s expiry is the only mechanism. Recommendation: call invalidate() from whatever deactivates an agent when that is built.

R-64-03 LOW OPEN Translation cache is keyed on md5 and has no workspace

It is content-addressed, so a reader only gets the translation of text it submitted. md5 collisions are practical but only let a sender affect how its own message is shown. Recommendation: sha256.

R-64-04 LOW OPEN Seed and demo commands do not bump the roles version

Offline commands that write user_roles leave running servers on cached grants for up to 600 s. Recommendation: call the bump or document the wait.

R-64-05 LOW OPEN SMS lookup verdict is kept 90 days with no invalidation

A number that changes carrier shows the old carrier. Informational tool; recommendation: 7 to 30 days.

Withdrawn after reading the code. D-64-03 (payment-driver maps never emptied) and D-64-04 (a FAQ cache without workspace) were not defects: the driver is created per call, and the embedding is content-addressed. They are on the allowlist or marked global with the reason.
Each ratchet seen to fail. Unit-level: 19 bad-example tests (an unbounded Map, an unregistered Map, a one-word reason, a key without org, a per-user key without user, a global key without a reason, an unfilled entry, SET without TTL, INCR then EXPIRE, a counter without expiry, an unregistered Redis writer, a public cache header, an unregistered grant writer; web: unregistered revalidate, a cookie-forwarding cached fetch, a soft sign-out). On the real code: a throw-away file with an unbounded Map and a Redis write failed two ratchets, then was deleted. Undoing one fix (webhook-target cap) made its regression test fail with "expected 750 to be 500".

6. Rollout and rollback

No staged deploy needed. One behaviour change to watch: counters now use a Redis transaction (MULTI/EXEC with EXPIRE ... NX, needs Redis 7; the code already used that form). Roll back by reverting the commit fix(api): set a counter's expiry....

7. What this does NOT prove

  • That caches are instrumented: nothing counts hits or misses (item #65).
  • That invalidation works end to end in a running system (item #66). The register lists the trigger for each cache; the RBAC part is tested against a real Redis, the rest with fakes.
  • Other apps: apps/partner and apps/mobile were not audited.
  • Redis writes made through names other than redis/client/conn (for example a store wrapper) are invisible to the scanner; BullMQ queue data is not a cache and was not audited.
  • Behaviour under a real multi-process deployment (two servers, clock skew) was reasoned about, not run.
  • Redis Cluster: the RBAC Lua script builds a key inside the script, so it needs a single Redis (already documented in the code).
  • The hit rate or memory use of any cache; sizes of the caps (500 to 10 000) are judgement, not measured.
  • The Postgres-backed tenancy audit controls did not execute in this environment (no database), and the architecture check has one error that exists on main (queue-guard imports a domain file).
  • Stale windows are the code's TTLs confirmed on a moving clock; real-world delay also includes the time a writer takes to call invalidate.
